name: Actinic Keratoses
overview: Actinic Keratoses (AK) are precancerous skin lesions caused by long-term ultraviolet (UV) radiation exposure. They represent abnormal growth of keratinocytes within the epidermis. Although many lesions remain stable for years, some can progress into invasive squamous cell carcinoma if left untreated. Early recognition and treatment significantly reduce the risk of malignant transformation.
description: Actinic Keratoses usually develop on chronically sun-exposed skin such as the face, scalp, ears, forearms, and hands. They often appear as rough, dry, or scaly patches that may be easier to feel than to see. Individual lesions are generally small but multiple lesions commonly occur in the same patient due to cumulative sun damage.
clinical_presentation: Persistent rough or scaly skin lesion
Pink, red, brown, or skin-colored appearance
typical_features: Chronic sun damage surrounding the lesion

ABCDE.Evolution: Slow enlargement or increasing roughness should be evaluated

diagnostic_workup: Skin biopsy if malignancy is suspected
prognosis: The prognosis is generally excellent when lesions are detected and treated early. Untreated lesions have a small but clinically significant risk of progressing to invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Long-term follow-up is recommended because new lesions commonly develop in sun-damaged skin.
next_steps: Document lesion size and appearance for future comparison.
Protect the affected area from further UV exposure.

follow_up.routine: Dermatology review every 6–12 months depending on individual risk.
follow_up.high_risk: Earlier review may be appropriate for high-risk individuals or if concerning changes occur.

patient_advice: Take photographs of the lesion to monitor changes over time.
Do not ignore persistent rough patches.
Use sunscreen every day, even during cloudy weather.
Seek medical evaluation if the lesion changes rapidly or develops bleeding or ulceration.
Continue routine skin examinations even after successful treatment.
